introduction.p: A Fourier series represents a periodic function using a constant and sine and cosine terms at integer multiples of a basic frequency. Integrals determine the coefficients by measuring these components. This section derives those formulas and works through examples; full convergence theory requires further results.

exercise.title: Why do Fourier series use waves instead of powers?

statement.p: Taylor series build functions from powers near a center. Fourier series build periodic functions from sines and cosines over a cycle. In your own words, why is that a different question, and why does the symbol \sim warn that having a Fourier series is not automatically the same as equaling it everywhere?

hint.p: Fourier coefficients describe frequency components rather than derivatives at a point. Convergence of the resulting series requires separate conditions, particularly at discontinuities.

subsection.title: Orthogonality of sine and cosine, geometrically
subsection.p: To find the coefficients in a Fourier series, we need a way to measure how much one function points in the direction of another.
For ordinary vectors, the dot product measures alignment. Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero.
For functions on [-\pi,\pi], the analogous dot product is an integral:
If
we say the functions are orthogonal on [-\pi,\pi].
This language is geometric. The functions are being treated like vectors, but with infinitely many coordinates.

exercise.title: Why do integrals measure how much of each wave is present?

statement.p: On [-\pi,\pi], the inner product of two functions is an integral, and distinct sine and cosine waves are orthogonal. In your own words, why is that the analogue of a dot product, and why does orthogonality let you extract one coefficient without the others interfering?

hint.p: Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero, so projection onto one direction ignores the others. Integrating a function against one wave is the same idea: the other waves contribute signed area zero over a full period.

description.p: Fourier partial sums approximate a square wave by adding sine waves. Near each jump, ripples remain.

subsection.p: The approximation improves away from the jumps. But near a jump, something strange happens. The partial sums overshoot the top level and undershoot the bottom level.
As we add more terms, the ripples get narrower. But the first overshoot near the jump does not simply disappear. It approaches a persistent limiting size.
This is called the Gibbs phenomenon.

note.title: Gibbs phenomenon
note.p: Fourier partial sums of a function with a jump often overshoot near the jump. Adding more terms makes the overshoot region narrower, but the overshoot height approaches a persistent limiting size.

subsection.p: There is also a convergence warning at the jump itself. The square wave jumps from -1 to 1 at t=0. The Fourier series does not choose the left value or the right value. It converges to the midpoint:
More generally, for a sufficiently well-behaved periodic function, the Fourier series converges at a jump to the average of the left-hand and right-hand limits.
The Fourier partial sums overshoot near a jump even as their values converge away from it. This behavior must be distinguished from pointwise convergence.

exercise.title: What does Gibbs phenomenon admit about jumps?

statement.p: For the square-wave example, Fourier partial sums overshoot near a jump and converge at the jump to the average of the two sides. Explain why this prevents uniform convergence and how it differs from Taylor representation.

hint.p: The jump is still visible in the approximation; the series does not pretend the function is continuous. Taylor series need local derivatives at a center, while Fourier coefficients are averages over a whole period.

subsection.title: Why Fourier series belong after Taylor series
subsection.p: Taylor series and Fourier series are cousins. Both try to build complicated functions from simple functions.
But they have different personalities.

subsection.p: A Taylor series asks:

p.me: \text{How does the function behave near one point?}

subsection.p: A Fourier series asks:

p.me: \text{What frequencies make up this repeating shape?}

subsection.p: Taylor coefficients come from derivatives at one point:
Fourier coefficients come from integrals over a whole period:
So Taylor series are local. Fourier series are global over a period.

This also explains why Fourier series can handle jumps better than Taylor series. A Taylor series is tied to local differentiability at a center. A Fourier series is built from waves and measures average alignment over an interval. It can still make sense when the function has corners or jumps.

subsection.p: The chapter began with a rotating exponential, reached vibrating springs, and then combined many waves. One more bridge remains. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus was the hinge of single-variable calculus. It also has a second life: it is the first example of a boundary theorem.

exercise.title: Why do Fourier series belong after Taylor series?

statement.p: Taylor coefficients come from derivatives at one point. Fourier coefficients come from integrals over a period. In your own words, why is one viewpoint local and the other global over a cycle, and how does Euler’s formula compress the real waves into complex exponentials?

hint.p: Local matching is the Taylor personality. Measuring frequencies over a whole loop is the Fourier personality. Since e^{int}=\cos(nt)+i\sin(nt), the two real families become one complex family.
